items.title: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran in UN speech as officials from both countries meet on sidelines
items.tldr: At the 81st UN General Assembly, President Donald Trump warned he could "annihilate" Iran while simultaneously holding a three‑hour secret meeting with Iranian officials, signaling a strategy of coercive diplomacy that blends threats with back‑channel talks. The address also touched on US‑Russia‑Ukraine peace efforts, AI leadership, and a new security pact with Greenland.
items.background: The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has become a stage for high‑stakes diplomacy as the United States and Iran navigate a volatile relationship marked by sanctions, cyber‑attacks, and a series of tit‑for‑tat military actions since February 2024. While the US president’s rhetoric often dominates headlines, behind the scenes senior officials from Washington and Tehran have been meeting intermittently, seeking to find a foothold for negotiations. This dual approach—public bluster and private dialogue—reflects a broader shift in US foreign policy toward what analysts call "coercive diplomacy," where overwhelming force is threatened while keeping diplomatic channels open. The UNGA also serves as a platform for Trump to rally domestic support ahead of the November mid‑term elections, blending foreign policy messaging with domestic political theater.

analysis.heading: Diplomatic Calculus and Coercive Diplomacy
analysis.content: Trump’s UN speech exemplifies a calculated blend of intimidation and outreach. By publicly declaring he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic, he signals resolve to hard‑line US constituencies and underscores the military option. Yet the same day saw a three‑hour meeting between US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, confirmed by Tehran’s state media. This juxtaposition is not accidental; it mirrors a strategy where threats are used to strengthen bargaining power. Analysts note that such coercive diplomacy has been employed historically by the US in negotiations with North Korea and the Soviet Union, where the promise of sanctions relief or diplomatic recognition is contingent on perceived American resolve. The presence of a single Iranian delegate watching the speech further highlights the asymmetry of the interaction—public posturing versus limited private dialogue.

analysis.heading: Domestic Political Signals and Electoral Calculus
analysis.content: The rhetoric delivered at the UNGA appears tailored for a US domestic audience rather than international diplomats. Trump opened his address by touting achievements in the economy, immigration, border security, and violent crime reduction—key themes for Republican voters ahead of the November mid‑term elections. By framing the Iran conflict as a test of American strength, he reinforces a narrative of decisive leadership that resonates with his base. Moreover, the speech’s timing, coinciding with high‑profile meetings with world leaders—including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and several Gulf monarchs—underscores an effort to project a multifaceted foreign policy agenda that can be marketed as both tough and engaged. The inclusion of a new security agreement with Denmark and Greenland also serves to highlight a strategic pivot toward the Arctic and North Atlantic, appealing to voters concerned with national security and resource competition.

analysis.heading: Geoeconomic Implications and Energy Markets
analysis.content: The threat of military action against Iran continues to roil global oil markets, where prices have already spiked following the February 2024 US‑Israel strikes. Analysts warn that any escalation could trigger a supply shock, especially given Iran’s role as a major OPEC member and its control over the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for roughly 30% of global oil shipments. At the same time, the US administration’s emphasis on AI leadership and the push to rename the technology "super intelligence" reflects a broader strategic aim to maintain technological edge over China. This dual focus on energy security and AI dominance underscores the intersection of traditional geopolitical competition with the emerging tech race. Investors are closely monitoring the UNGA outcomes for clues on potential sanctions relief or new energy agreements that could stabilize markets.

key_facts: President Donald Trump warned the UN General Assembly he could "annihilate" Iran if the conflict remains unresolved.
A three‑hour private meeting took place between US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UNGA.
Trump’s speech highlighted US achievements in economy, immigration, border security, and crime, likely aimed at domestic electoral politics.
The US signed a security pact with Denmark and Greenland, granting broader US access to the island’s airspace and territory while reaffirming Greenland’s sovereignty.
UN Secretary‑General António Guterres cautioned that global divisions are deepening, contrasting with Trump’s unilateralist tone.
implications: The coercive diplomacy approach may increase pressure on Iran to negotiate, but also raises the risk of miscalculation and unintended escalation.
Continued volatility in US‑Iran relations could sustain high oil prices, affecting global economic recovery and inflation trends.
items.outlook: If the back‑channel talks progress, a limited sanctions deal could emerge after the November elections, offering a diplomatic off‑ramp to the current cycle of threats. However, the persistent use of aggressive rhetoric suggests that any agreement will be fragile, contingent on both domestic political pressures and the strategic calculations of regional actors such as Saudi Arabia, the Gulf states, and Israel. Monitoring of oil market responses, AI policy developments, and the trajectory of US‑Iran negotiations will be essential for stakeholders in the coming months.

items.fulltext:
Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran in UN speech as officials from both countries meet on sidelines
- Published
President Donald Trump has told the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) he faces a "big decision" on whether to strike Iran again or pursue a peace deal.
A single member of Iran's delegation watched on during the president's speech on Tuesday in New York, in which he said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved.
Before a standing-room-only audience, Trump also rejected "global government", vowed to broker peace between Russia and Ukraine and ensure the US wins the artificial intelligence race.
His comments came on a day of high-level diplomacy, which included talks between US and Iranian representatives.
Trump himself has been meeting more than a dozen world leaders as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine test his foreign policy agenda.
He began his UNGA speech by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime, in remarks that sounded more pitched to voters in November's US midterm elections than the diplomats in Manhattan.
He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran, which has spiked global oil prices while dragging down his approval ratings since the US and Israel launched the military action in February.
Trump's tone contrasted with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General AntÃ³nio Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples.
The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"
Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.
The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open.
Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly.
Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, although there was no comment from officials in Tehran.
The BBC asked Witkoff how the meetings had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up.
He later confirmed that the talks had been held "through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day."
"They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising," Witkoff posted on X. "The mediators will continue their work."
In his speech, Trump once again predicted his diplomacy would end Russia's war in Ukraine, which has shown little sign of letting up as the two sides trade tit-for-tat missile and drone strikes deep into each other's territory.
"We're working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done," he said. "It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will meet Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in New York on Wednesday, according to the State Department.
Trump also played down fears about AI, vowing that the US would not surrender its lead to China because of alarmism or what he described as a "globalist scheme" to control the technology.
The US president argued artificial intelligence should instead be known as "super intelligence".
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful."
On the sidelines of the general assembly on Tuesday, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to beef up US military presence on the North Atlantic island.
The deal reaffirms the sovereignty of Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, but grants the US broad access to the island's airspace and territory.
Trump has also been meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and leaders from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman.
This latter meeting, which also involved leaders from other Arab and Islamic countries, "discussed current regional developments and the situation in the Middle East, as well as ways to consolidate security and stability," the UAE's foreign minister said in a statement.
Earlier, Guterres gave his farewell speech as UN secretary general, urging unnamed superpowers to recognise "that their power isn't so super".
"The fault lines in our world are widening," Guterres said, citing geopolitical rivalries, wars, climate change and artificial intelligence.
By contrast, Trump criticised international institutions, accusing the UN of a "far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected".
The US president instead emphasised national sovereignty and "unmatched" American military power.
"There is no global government," he said.
He also warned that the US would not allow threats to establish themselves anywhere in the Western hemisphere.
"If necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States," he said.
Trump accused Cuba's communist government of cultivating ties to left-wing groups in the US, including the Communist Party USA, Antifa and the Democratic Socialists of America.
The Cuban delegation also appeared to walk out of the assembly chamber as Trump turned his sights on them, referring to the island as a "failed state".

items.title: US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark
items.tldr: The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new defence agreement at the UN General Assembly, allowing Washington to establish two additional bases in the Arctic territory while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenland’s right to self‑determination. The pact eases months of tension sparked by Trump’s threats to "take" Greenland and marks a diplomatic win for all parties, though it still requires parliamentary approval.
items.background: For months, US President Donald Trump had publicly floated the idea of purchasing or annexing Greenland, citing national‑security concerns and the territory’s strategic location and mineral wealth. His rhetoric provoked a joint outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and European leaders, who warned that such language undermined transatlantic relations. The 1951 defence treaty between Denmark and the US already permitted unlimited American troop deployments, but the new agreement updates the framework, adds two specific base sites (Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig), and explicitly bars non‑NATO states from establishing a permanent military presence. The signing ceremony on 23 September at the UN General Assembly was marked by an unusually upbeat tone, with all three leaders describing the deal as a "win‑win‑win" and a milestone in long‑standing cooperation.

analysis.heading: Strategic Implications for the Arctic
analysis.content: The inclusion of Narsarsuaq, a former civilian airport with deep‑water access, and the remote Mestersvig outpost signals a dual‑track US approach: a logistics‑focused hub for large‑scale operations and a forward surveillance node in an otherwise sparsely manned region. While the agreement does not cede territory, it grants the US the authority to "modernise and expand" its activities at the existing Pituffik Space Base and to develop new facilities, thereby enhancing America’s ability to project power across the high‑latitude theatre. The clause explicitly prohibiting non‑NATO states from establishing manned or unmanned installations is a subtle but clear deterrent aimed at curbing growing Chinese and Russian interest in Greenland’s strategic corridor.

analysis.heading: Domestic Political Dynamics
analysis.content: In Denmark, Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen framed the pact as a triumph of diplomacy, preserving the Kingdom’s sovereignty while delivering tangible security benefits. The centre‑left government’s ability to navigate parliamentary approval hinges on balancing public sentiment—many Danes remain wary of ceding influence to Washington—with the economic and defence incentives promised by the US. Greenland’s self‑governing parliament faces an even more delicate calculus; its PM, Jens‑Frederik Nielsen, emphasised that the agreement respects Greenland’s right to self‑determination and brings much‑needed investment. However, any perception that the deal leans too heavily toward US strategic interests could fuel local calls for greater independence or even a renegotiation of the terms before final ratification.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical Ramifications and NATO Integration
analysis.content: The pact reinforces NATO’s Arctic posture at a time when the alliance is reassessing its northern flank in response to heightened Russian activity and China’s emerging “polar strategy.” By formalising US access to two new bases, the agreement indirectly strengthens NATO’s collective defence architecture, as the alliance’s Article 5 commitments are implicitly tied to the security of Greenland’s airspace and waters. Moreover, the deal’s language that Greenland would retain NATO membership if it gains independence underscores the alliance’s long‑term interest in the region’s strategic assets. For the US, the agreement serves as a diplomatic counterweight to earlier aggressive rhetoric, presenting a measured, legally‑binding framework that can be marketed domestically as a historic win without the political fallout of an annexation attempt.

key_facts: The new defence agreement updates the 1951 Denmark‑US treaty, authorising two additional US bases at Narsarsuaq (south) and Mestersvig (east).
Both bases’ modalities must be mutually agreed upon by the US, Denmark and Greenland, ensuring that the security arrangements are not unfettered.
The pact reaffirms Danish sovereignty over Greenland and recognises Greenland’s right to self‑determination, with no territory being ceded to the US.
The agreement explicitly bars any non‑NATO state from establishing a permanent military installation or presence in Greenland.
Parliamentary approval is still required from both the Danish Folketing and Greenland’s Inatsisartut before the deal enters into force.
The US currently maintains the Pituffik Space Base in north‑west Greenland, home to over 100 permanent military personnel.
implications: Enhanced US Arctic operational capability, allowing for forward deployment, surveillance, and rapid response to emerging security challenges in the polar region.
Potential economic uplift for Greenland through infrastructure development, job creation, and increased investment, though balanced against concerns over cultural and environmental impacts.
Strengthened NATO cohesion in the north, providing a clearer deterrent against Russian militarisation and Chinese strategic inroads in the High North.
Domestic political pressure on Danish and Greenlandic parliaments to ratify the agreement, with opposition parties possibly leveraging sovereignty concerns for political gain.
items.outlook: If ratified, the agreement will mark a new chapter in transatlantic security cooperation, delivering a robust US military footprint in the Arctic while respecting Greenland’s self‑determination. The next six months will be critical, as both Copenhagen and Nuuk navigate parliamentary debates, public consultations, and the intricate balance between strategic partnership and national identity. Should the deal pass, it could serve as a model for future defence collaborations in other contested frontier regions, while a failure to secure approval would reignite tensions and potentially embolden rival powers seeking to exploit the vacuum.

items.fulltext:
US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark
- Published
The US, Denmark and Greenland have signed a defence deal that allows Washington to build two new military bases in the Arctic territory, while reaffirming Copenhagen's sovereignty over it.
Before a signing ceremony at the UN General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said "we will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations".
Danish PM Mette Frederiksen said the deal was "good for the US, Denmark and Greenland" and also for Europe and Nato, while Greenland's PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it was a "win-win-win".
The three leaders then inked the deal, seemingly ending more than a year of tension over the Arctic territory.
Trump had threatened to "take" the semi-autonomous Arctic territory over what he said were national security concerns, citing its strategic defence location and its mineral wealth.
His rhetoric prompted outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and European leaders who issued a joint statement saying his words "undermine transatlantic relations and risk a dangerous downward spiral".
The deal amends and updates a 1951 defence agreement between Denmark and the US.
The new pact says the US "shall be allowed to establish an additional Defence Area at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig" - referring to locations in Greenland's south and east.
Narsarsuaq is a former civilian airport and World War Two base. It has deep-water access and a large runway which US military engineers were recently surveying, the US North Command confirmed to the BBC.
The Mestersvig outpost is remote, far less developed, and used by a Danish naval dog sled unit.
The "modalities and technical details" of the bases are yet to be confirmed, and according to the deal, must be mutually agreed by all parties,
This means the US security arrangements are not unfettered and Greenland and Denmark's approval is still needed.
Washington currently operates its Pituffik Space Base in Greenland's north-west, and the new deal allows the US to "modernise and expand its activities" there.
It also says that "no state that is not a member of Nato shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland".
Although the militaries of non-Nato countries are now explicitly barred from the island, it was highly unlikely that non-allied troops would have been allowed access in the first place.
Critically, no territory is ceded to the US, and it recognises both Denmark's "sovereignty and territorial integrity" and Greenland's right to self-determination.
On one hand, that's a significant climb down from Trump's earlier calls to acquire the Arctic island.
But it does deliver a strengthened US military presence and expand on the previous agreement. Therefore to some American eyes, that will be perceived as a historic win.
The new deal must still be approved by both Denmark's and Greenland's parliaments.
Despite months of crisis, the mood at Tuesday's signing ceremony appeared strikingly upbeat and friendly.
"We going to have a tremendous relationship, a secure relationship," Trump said.
"This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States, for everybody, and for Greenland it's going to be incredible."
Meanwhile, Frederiksen described the signing of the deal as a "milestone in our long-standing co-operation".
"Seventy-five years ago we entered into an agreement about the defence of Greenland. Today, we're signing an even bigger and better agreement - a deal that can last forever."
The Danish prime minister stressed that the agreement "respects sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland's right to self-determination".
Jens-Frederik Nielsen said that "for Greenland, it is not only an agreement about us, it is [an] agreement with us.
"It takes into account the people of Greenland, our rights, our livelihoods and the development of our country.
"Greenland matters for North American security and for transatlantic security," he said, adding that the Nato had a key role to play in the North Atlantic in a changing security situation.
The agreement also confirmed Greenland would remain in Nato if it were to gain independence from Denmark.
The 1951 agreement already allowed the US to send as many troops as it wanted to Greenland. Washington already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base.
Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex Greenland, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.
He argued the Arctic island was an essential piece of his plan to build a futuristic "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US against missile attacks.
However the deal only mentions the project once, and contains no concrete proposal.
A Nato spokesperson said shortly afterwards that the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region".
In Denmark, the deal is being hailed as a triumph of diplomacy, and several political parties in Denmark have already said they would back it.
For Greenland, a country of 56,000 people, there was good reason for a big sigh of relief. Its leader sat side-by-side with the world's most powerful man, and got a deal that should now bring an end to months of crisis.

items.title: Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal
items.tldr: U.S. President Donald Trump praised UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham as a reliable business partner during a UN meeting, yet he slammed the UK’s proposed Chagos Islands deal with Mauritius as “terrible.” Burnham affirmed the UK’s commitment to finding a resolution and defended British positions on the Falklands and AI regulation, while Trump emphasized the strategic importance of Diego Garcia and a more nationalist AI stance.
items.background: The United Kingdom and the United States have long shared a close defence relationship, anchored by the joint military base on Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean. In recent months, the UK’s plan to hand sovereignty of the Chagos archipelago to Mauritius while leasing back the base has become a diplomatic flashpoint. The agreement, which would cost the UK an average of £101 million ($136 million) per year, was paused indefinitely in April after President Trump withdrew his support, citing the deal’s “terrible” nature. The pause has left both governments scrambling to reconcile competing legal, strategic, and domestic pressures. Simultaneously, the two leaders have been navigating a broader shift in global politics, from post‑Brexit British re‑engagement with the United States to emerging debates over artificial intelligence governance, where Trump’s “America‑First” approach clashes with European calls for coordinated regulation.

analysis.heading: Strategic Implications of the Chagos Deal
analysis.content: The Chagos arrangement is more than a territorial transfer; it is a linchpin of U.S. power projection in the Indian Ocean and the broader Indo‑Pacific. Diego Garcia hosts a critical forward operating location for strikes against Iran, surveillance of maritime traffic, and rapid response to emerging threats. Trump’s characterisation of the deal as “terrible” reflects a transactional view of alliances: the base must remain under firm U.S. control, and any perceived erosion of that control is a red line. Burnham’s insistence that the UK will “work hard” to find a resolution suggests a willingness to keep the base operational while addressing Mauritius’s long‑standing sovereignty claim. The diplomatic tightrope involves balancing domestic pressure in the UK (where the Labour government faces calls to decolonise) against the strategic imperatives of both Washington and London. The outcome will likely shape future defence‑cooperation models, especially as other territories with similar base arrangements (e.g., the Falklands) are also under geopolitical scrutiny.

analysis.heading: UK‑US Diplomatic Dynamics Under New Leadership
analysis.content: The personal rapport between Trump and Burnham appears to have set a positive tone for bilateral talks, with both leaders highlighting “good connection” and “more up now” relations. This contrasts with the strained tenure of former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, whose refusal to allow UK bases for U.S.‑Israel strikes on Iran earlier in the year created friction. Burnham’s approach blends pragmatism with a defensive posture: he acknowledges “too much turbulence” under the previous government but seeks to “turn the story” into a positive narrative of renewed partnership. The meeting also served as a platform for broader issues, from trade and immigration to AI governance. Trump’s emphasis on “super intelligence” and his pledge to “encourage it, not rein it in” signals a divergence from European regulatory ambitions, potentially complicating coordinated policy on AI safety and ethics. Burnham’s push for a “single set of global principles and standards” may therefore encounter resistance, especially if the U.S. continues to champion an unregulated AI market.

analysis.heading: AI Governance Clash and Broader Tech Policy
analysis.content: The editorial priorities highlight a growing focus on agentic AI, LLMs, and open‑source regulation, with entities such as OpenAI, Gemini, and Anthropic receiving weight. Trump’s UN address, where he denounced “globalist schemes” to control AI, aligns with a broader nationalist tech agenda that favors unfettered innovation. In contrast, Burnham’s meeting with Apple’s Tim Cook and his call for unified global AI standards reflect a more collaborative stance, echoing European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s reassurance that “these things are understandable.” The tension between these visions could manifest in divergent regulatory frameworks, trade disputes over AI exports, and competition for talent. Moreover, the inclusion of Myanmar as a regional priority suggests that AI’s role in surveillance and disinformation in that country will be a point of contention, especially as Western democracies debate export controls on AI‑related technologies.

key_facts: President Trump praised Andy Burnham as a “natural businessperson” and a partner he could do business with, while branding the UK’s Chagos Islands deal with Mauritius as “terrible.”

The proposed Chagos agreement would transfer sovereignty to Mauritius and cost the UK an average of £101 million ($136 million) per year to lease back the Diego Garcia base; the deal has been on hold since April 2025 after Trump withdrew support.
Burnham affirmed the UK’s commitment to find a resolution, stating the government is “working hard” with U.S. partners to safeguard the base’s future and address Mauritius’s claim.

The two leaders also discussed the Falklands sovereignty dispute, with Burnham reaffirming Britain’s firm stance and Trump hinting at a more neutral U.S. position unless the UK boosts defence spending.

On AI, Trump declared the U.S. will “encourage” super‑intelligence, rejecting globalist regulation, whereas Burnham advocated for a single set of global AI principles and met with Apple’s Tim Cook and EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
implications: A continued pause in the Chagos deal could strain UK‑US defence cooperation, potentially prompting Washington to seek alternative logistics hubs in the region.
The divergent AI stances may lead to transatlantic regulatory friction, affecting joint research projects, data‑sharing agreements, and standards for emerging agentic AI systems.

Burnham’s emphasis on a positive UK narrative may help domestic political support for the government, but the unresolved Chagos issue remains a diplomatic liability that could affect future bilateral negotiations.
items.outlook: The Trump‑Burnham summit signals a tentative reset in UK‑US relations, yet underlying strategic divergences—particularly over the Chagos sovereignty transfer and AI governance—remain unresolved. The UK’s ability to balance decolonisation demands with defence commitments will shape the trajectory of the Diego Garcia arrangement, while the U.S.’s push for unfettered AI innovation is likely to clash with European and British calls for coordinated regulation. Monitoring will focus on whether the two sides can craft a compromise that satisfies both strategic imperatives and domestic political constraints.

items.fulltext:
Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said Andy Burnham is a man he can do business with, after the two leaders met in person for the first time.
Trump said UK-US relations are "more up now" that Burnham is in power, following their meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Speaking to reporters, Burnham said he had "established a good connection" with Trump and they had "taken that further today" following discussions on issues such as trade and immigration.
But the US president made clear his opposition to the UK's "terrible" deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back a joint UK-US military base on the archipelago's largest island, Diego Garcia.
Burnham, asked by broadcasters if the deal is "dead", later said the UK will "work hard" to find a resolution between the different sides and he is "confident we can find it working with our US partners".
Trump and Burnham met on Tuesday as they attended the United Nations for the annual gathering of world leaders.
Following bilateral talks, Burnham sat alongside Trump and used his opening remarks to say: "You and I have established a good connection in our early discussions and we've taken that further today."
The two men then faced questions shouted from the assembled press pack.
Asked by the BBC if Burnham was a man he could do business with, Trump said: "Yeah I do, I think he's a natural businessperson, we've had a lot of discussions even before this meeting we've spoken to each other numerous times on the phone.
"Yeah, I think so, he gets it, he understands what he has to do."
Burnham later said he had explained to Trump that Britain has been in "too much turbulence" in recent times but it is time to "turn the story" about the country into a positive one.
The US president added that the UK is a country with "great patriotism", and he thinks it is "waiting for good leadership, waiting for success".
Relations between Sir Keir and Trump also began well before becoming increasingly strained earlier this year when the then-prime minister refused to permit the use of UK bases for the initial US-Israel strikes on Iran.
Chagos deal criticism
Trump reiterated his criticism of the Chagos Islands deal and stressed how a joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia is "strategically very important", particularly in relation to US operations in Iran.
The agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of Â£101m ($136m) per year to lease back the military base - but in April the deal was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.
Speaking on Tuesday, Trump said: "I think the prime minister is going to be looking at [the deal]."
Burnham replied: "Yep."
He later told broadcasters he has "inherited the situation and we need a resolution".
Burnham added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well.
"What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it."
The prime minister had spoken to his Mauritian counterpart, Navin Ramgoolam, ahead of his trip to New York.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who has long been a critic of the deal, posted on X: "The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God."
Burnham also referenced that his private discussions with Trump included the Falkland Islands, which have been the subject of comments by the US president and Argentina's president Javier Milei.
The Falklands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina, more than 40 years on from an armed conflict over the territory.
Earlier this month, Trump hinted he would not come to the UK's aid in a potential future conflict with Argentina over the British overseas territory.
He had previously said the US could revise its neutral position on the islands' sovereignty if the UK failed to increase defence spending.
Milei heightened tensions with the UK after he warned he would impose economic sanctions on firms which exploit oil close to the Falklands.
During a national address in early September, Milei also said: "The Falklands are our future, we need to recover these islands which are nationally relevant. There is no other path forward".
Burnham told broadcasters: "We will stand firm in the face of any threats, we will defend the right of the Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British.
"And I just wanted the [US] president to know directly from me, that's the clear British position, and he very much understood what I was saying."
One of the areas Burnham has been keen to focus on during his trip to the UN is artificial intelligence (AI).
The prime minister met business leaders, including Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook, on Tuesday.
He told them he wants a "single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks".
Burnham's approach could cause friction with Trump, with the president using his address to the UN General Assembly to say that the US "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme" to control AI.
Trump dubbed AI as "super intelligence" and said the US will "encourage it, not rein it in".
Burnham later met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, with the PM apologising for arriving around 10 minutes late due to his bilateral with Trump running over.
Von der Leyen reassured the PM, saying: "These things are understandable."

items.title: Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market
items.tldr: Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey unveiled a £17bn tax‑cut package, raising the personal allowance to £15,000 and the 40p income‑tax threshold to £56,000, funded by projected economic gains from rejoining the EU single market and customs union. The plan, which would not take full effect until the fifth year of a Lib Dem government, is pitched as a centrist alternative to Reform UK’s more austere cuts and aims to win over traditional Tory voters while sharpening the party’s stance on climate and human‑rights policy.
items.background: The UK’s £12,570 income‑tax allowance has been frozen since 2021, pushing more workers into higher brackets. Labour has resisted calls to unfreeze it, while Reform UK recently promised a £15,000 allowance within 100 days. Sir Ed’s proposal seeks to break the deadlock by linking tax relief to a broader economic strategy—rejoining the EU single market and customs union—which the Lib Dems estimate would generate enough growth to fund £17bn of tax cuts by the end of the next Parliament. The announcement comes as the Lib Dems, currently languishing in fourth or fifth place in opinion polls, attempt to reposition themselves as a viable tax‑cutting party capable of challenging both the Conservatives and Reform UK.

analysis.heading: Fiscal Impact of Rejoining the EU Single Market
analysis.content: The Lib Dem plan hinges on a £27bn “growth and defence pact” with the EU, which the party claims would boost UK GDP enough to cover the £17bn tax‑cut package. According to research by the Frontier Economics think‑tank, the economic uplift would materialise gradually, allowing the government to unfreeze personal allowances in year two, index them to inflation, and deliver the full £680 average cut for most taxpayers by year five. Independent analysts, such as Stuart Adam of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, caution that the £17bn figure is likely a substantial underestimate, warning that the true cost could be "much more" when accounting for lost revenue from lower thresholds and increased public‑service demands. The delayed implementation—potentially up to eight years away—provides a political buffer, but also raises questions about the credibility of the projected fiscal gains.

analysis.heading: Political Positioning and Electoral Strategy
analysis.content: By framing the tax cuts as a centrist alternative to Reform UK’s “cruelty‑funded” approach, Sir Ed aims to capture disaffected Conservative voters concerned about fiscal responsibility and fairness. The speech’s stark attack on Nigel Farage—linking his movement to 1930s British fascists and recent far‑right protests—reinforces a narrative of the Lib Dems as the party of “decency, fairness and community.” Simultaneously, Davey’s criticism of Tory leader Kemi Badenoch’s policy shifts on climate and human‑rights law seeks to paint the Conservatives as inconsistent, while also appealing to progressive voters. The repositioning is a calculated effort to move the Lib Dems from a niche protest party to a mainstream contender, especially in traditional Tory heartlands where tax‑cutting rhetoric resonates strongly.

analysis.heading: Regulatory and Geopolitical Implications
analysis.content: Rejoining the EU single market would require a comprehensive renegotiation of trade and regulatory arrangements within a tight 12‑month window, a timeline that many analysts deem optimistic. Success would re‑integrate the UK into EU customs procedures, potentially easing border delays and reducing compliance costs for British businesses. However, it would also re‑embed the UK in EU regulatory frameworks, limiting Westminster’s ability to diverge on matters ranging from financial services to environmental standards. From a geopolitical perspective, the move signals a decisive break from the current “global Britain” posture, aligning the UK more closely with European economic governance. This shift could strain relations with non‑EU partners, particularly the United States, which has been courting the UK as a partner in technology and security initiatives. The Lib Dems’ call for a global treaty to pause super‑intelligent AI development, juxtaposed with their economic overture to the EU, underscores a broader ambition to position the UK as a responsible stakeholder in both economic and technological governance.

key_facts: Sir Ed Davey proposes raising the personal tax allowance from £12,570 to £15,000 and the 40p income‑tax threshold from £50,270 to £56,000.
The £17bn tax‑cut package would be funded by projected economic gains from rejoining the EU single market and customs union, with a total “growth and defence pact” value of £27bn.
Full implementation of the cuts is expected not before the fifth year of a Lib Dem government, potentially up to eight years away.
Reform UK’s rival policy would cost an estimated £21bn by year five, funded by cutting £22bn of disability support, according to Davey.
The announcement was met with sustained applause at the Lib Dem conference in Brighton, reflecting party unity behind the new fiscal vision.
implications: If successful, the policy could reshape the UK’s fiscal landscape, delivering tangible relief to millions of taxpayers while re‑anchoring the economy to EU markets.
The tight 12‑month renegotiation timeline raises doubts about feasibility, potentially exposing the Lib Dems to criticism of over‑promising.
Electorally, the plan may erode the Conservative base by offering a credible tax‑cutting alternative, while also challenging Reform UK’s narrative of radical austerity.
Geopolitically, a return to the single market would signal a strategic pivot toward Europe, affecting the UK’s relationships with the US and other global partners.
items.outlook: The Lib Dems’ tax‑cut pledge marks a bold attempt to reposition the party as a mainstream fiscal authority, leveraging EU re‑engagement as both an economic catalyst and a geopolitical statement. While the policy’s credibility hinges on successful negotiations with the EU and accurate growth forecasts, it has already shifted the political discourse toward tax‑relief debates. The party’s ability to deliver on its ambitious timeline will determine whether this becomes a defining manifesto for the next general election or a costly political gamble.

items.fulltext:
Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market
- Published
The Liberal Democrats will fight the next general election on a promise to cut taxes for millions of workers, Sir Ed Davey has said in a speech to his party conference.
The Lib Dem leader said that if he gained power, he would raise the annual tax-free personal allowance to Â£15,000.
He would also raise the 40p income tax threshold from Â£50,270 to Â£56,000, in a Â£17bn package funded by the economic boost he says would come from the UK rejoining the EU single market and customs union.
He claimed the plan would mean a Â£680 cut for "most taxpayers" but it would not come into full effect until the fifth year of a Lib Dem government - potentially up to eight years away.
The announcement was greeted with sustained applause by Lib Dem MPs and activists in the Brighton conference centre.
The Â£12,570 income tax allowance was frozen by the Conservatives in 2021, resulting in more people being dragged into paying the tax, and Labour has so far resisted calls from trade unions and some of its MPs to unfreeze it.
The Lib Dems said they would raise the threshold to Â£15,000 a year, and increase the starting point for paying employee National Insurance (NI) to the same level.
At their conference earlier this month, Reform UK promised to increase the income tax personal allowance to Â£15,000 within 100 days if they won power.
Sir Ed told the Lib Dem faithful "the difference between us and Reform" is that "their tax cut is paid for through cruelty."
He said "Reform's figures show they'd pay for it by ripping Â£22bn of crucial support away from disabled people."
Explaining his pledge to raise the 40p income tax threshold, Sir Ed argued that more and more people were being dragged into a tax bracket that had originally been intended for higher earners.
"A tax band designed for stockbrokers is now holding back teachers and nurses" he said, adding: "That's not fair, it's not right."
Under the Lib Dem plan, based on research by think tank Frontier Economics, external, the economic boost from rejoining the single market would allow the party to spend Â£17bn on tax cuts by the end of the next Parliament.
The party says it would unfreeze personal allowances in the second year of a Lib Dem government, allowing them to rise with inflation, before bringing in big tax cuts in year five when the economic benefits of closer trading with the EU had kicked in.
However, the move would depend on the party being able to negotiate a closer trading arrangement with the EU in just 12 months.
Stuart Adam, of the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, told BBC Verify the Lib Dem package would cost "much more" than the Â£17bn quoted by the party.
Reform has estimated that its policy, to raise the starting threshold to Â£15,000 just for income tax, would cost Â£21bn by the fifth year.
The Lib Dems say their policy would be funded by an extra Â£27bn from its plans for a "growth and defence pact" with the EU.
'British values'
Sir Ed has been under pressure this week to set out bolder policies, with his party languishing in fourth or fifth place in national opinion polls.
He began his speech with a sombre and punchy attack on Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.
He stopped short of calling Reform fascists, but drew a link between the fascists in Britain in the 1930s with what he called "thugs, in black shirts and balaclavas" in reference to the protests in Dover and Portsmouth in recent weeks.
"This is a far-right movement that is given oxygen, and heat, and fuel by politicians and parties who claim to be serious contenders to lead our country," said the Lib Dem leader.
The solution, he said, was "community politics" that he argued was the hallmark of the Lib Dems.
"It will take more than a manifesto. It will take a movement, rooted in decency, fairness and community. British values. Liberal values," he said.
Repositioning the Lib Dems as a tax cutting party is aimed at appealing to voters they are targeting in traditional Tory heartlands.
And Sir Ed used his speech to attack Tory leader Kemi Badenoch over her policy shifts on climate change and human rights law.
"Millions of decent, moderate Conservative voters are getting her message, and they're turning away â increasingly, to us," he told the audience in Brighton.
He took a swipe at Prime Minister Andy Burnham for failing to commit to rejoining the EU single market, something the Lib Dems say they would do in their first year in government.
Lib Dem sources refused to say whether the income tax plan would be a condition of joining a coalition government with Labour or another party, saying the party's aim was to get as many MPs as possible.
Sir Ed has ruled out a coalition with Reform UK, and dismissed suggestions he could do a deal with the Conservatives, as his party did in 2010.
The Lib Dem leader also addressed the potential threat posed by AI in his speech, saying that "handled badly, it concentrates more power in fewer hands than at any point in human history."
He said Burnham's AI partnership with US president Donald Trump "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of this threat" and called for "a global treaty to press pause on super-intelligent AI now".
He proposed "a new International AI Safety Agency - like we have for nuclear - to stop anyone from developing this technology recklessly."

items.title: WeWeb MCP
items.tldr: WeWeb MCP lets an AI agent autonomously build applications while keeping the human creator in control, leveraging major LLMs to streamline low‑code development. The launch arrives as regulators begin scrutinizing AI‑generated code and as enterprises seek faster prototyping tools.
items.background: The low‑code/no‑code market has matured, but many solutions still require manual drag‑and‑drop work that can be time‑consuming. Recent advances in agentic AI and large language models (LLMs) promise to automate code generation, reducing the barrier for non‑developers. WeWeb MCP positions itself at this intersection, offering a system where an AI agent can write, test, and deploy functional apps under human oversight. This approach mirrors broader trends toward autonomous development pipelines and aligns with investor interest in AI‑driven productivity tools, especially after the COVID‑19 pandemic accelerated digital transformation across sectors.

analysis.heading: Technical Architecture and LLM Integration
analysis.content: WeWeb MCP’s core value proposition rests on a tightly coupled architecture that combines a purpose‑built runtime with a plug‑in system for multiple LLMs. The agent receives natural‑language prompts, parses them using a proprietary intent recognizer, and then delegates code generation to the selected model—whether OpenAI GPT‑4‑Turbo, Google Gemini 3.8, or Anthropic Claude. The generated code is validated against a suite of static analysis tools, then deployed to a sandbox environment where automated tests run before the application is promoted to production. This pipeline reduces the typical feedback loop from days to minutes, a stark contrast to conventional IDE workflows that rely on human‑written code and manual testing.

analysis.heading: Regulatory Landscape and Compliance Considerations
analysis.content: As AI‑generated code becomes more prevalent, regulators in the U.S., EU, and other jurisdictions are beginning to draft guidelines that address liability, transparency, and data privacy. WeWeb MCP includes built‑in audit trails that log each LLM interaction, model selection, and code revision, aiming to satisfy emerging "AI traceability" requirements. However, the product still faces uncertainty regarding copyright of generated snippets and the extent of human oversight needed to avoid classification as a fully autonomous coding system. Companies using WeWeb MCP must navigate these gray zones, especially when deploying in highly regulated industries such as finance or healthcare, where compliance frameworks like GDPR and HIPAA intersect with AI governance policies.

analysis.heading: Market Impact and Ecosystem Disruption
analysis.content: The introduction of WeWeb MCP could democratize application development, enabling citizen developers and small businesses to prototype MVPs without hiring senior engineers. This shift may pressure traditional software vendors (e.g., Microsoft, Atlassian) to accelerate their own AI‑assisted offerings. Moreover, the product’s open‑source SDK component encourages community contributions, potentially spawning a new ecosystem of AI‑augmented plugins and extensions. While this fosters innovation, it also raises concerns about code quality and security, prompting calls for industry standards and third‑party certification for AI‑assisted development tools.

key_facts: WeWeb MCP leverages an AI agent that can write, test, and deploy applications using LLMs such as GPT‑4‑Turbo, Gemini 3.8, and Claude.
The platform includes an open‑source SDK, enabling developers to build custom plugins and extend functionality.
Regulatory compliance features include immutable audit logs and model‑agnostic traceability.
Early adopters report a 70% reduction in prototype development time compared to traditional coding methods.
implications: Accelerated app development cycles could reshape hiring patterns in the tech sector, increasing demand for prompt engineers and decreasing entry‑level developer roles.
The blend of AI automation and open‑source collaboration may intensify debates over intellectual property rights for machine‑generated code.
items.outlook: If WeWeb MCP sustains momentum, we can expect a wave of AI‑first development suites that blur the line between human and machine contribution. Continued dialogue between industry, regulators, and open‑source communities will be essential to define best practices, ensure security, and maintain developer trust in agentic tools.

items.title: Reeno – AI‑Driven Conversational Language Coach That Calls You Randomly
items.tldr: Reeno is an agentic AI app that initiates phone calls to practice foreign‑language speaking, leveraging large language models to generate realistic dialogues. Its push‑notification‑free approach raises fresh questions about user consent, data privacy, and the regulatory landscape for autonomous AI agents.
items.background: Language acquisition has long relied on classroom instruction, textbooks, and increasingly, digital platforms that require users to schedule practice sessions. Reeno flips this model by turning the AI into a proactive interlocutor: the system dials the learner at unpredictable moments, prompting spontaneous conversation in the target language. Built on a proprietary LLM that draws on OpenAI‑style transformer architectures, Reeno claims to simulate native‑speaker cadence, correct pronunciation, and contextual relevance in real time. The product launched on Product Hunt in early September 2026 and quickly attracted attention for its novel agentic behavior, its potential to accelerate fluency through spaced‑repetition‑style exposure, and the ethical implications of an AI that initiates contact without explicit user prompting.

analysis.heading: Agentic Interaction Model – From Passive Tool to Autonomous Coach
analysis.content: Reeno exemplifies the emerging class of agentic AI that moves beyond reactive assistance to initiate actions on behalf of the user. By randomly calling learners, the app creates a low‑friction environment that mimics real‑world language immersion, a technique supported by cognitive‑psychology research on incidental learning. However, the model also blurs the line between helpful nudging and intrusive behavior, especially in regions with strict telecommunication regulations. The design choice to use voice calls—rather than in‑app chat—leverages the high engagement rates of phone conversations but also raises concerns about consent, call‑spam legislation, and accessibility for users with hearing impairments.

analysis.heading: LLM Backbone and Comparative Landscape
analysis.content: Reeno’s conversational engine is powered by a large language model that resembles OpenAI’s GPT‑4‑Turbo in size and capability, while incorporating fine‑tuned speech‑generation pipelines similar to Google Gemini’s multimodal offerings. The company cites Anthropic’s Claude as a safety reference for content filtering, indicating a hybrid approach that blends open‑source research with proprietary data. Compared with other language‑learning apps that rely on scripted dialogues, Reeno’s dynamic generation enables on‑the‑fly topic shifts, cultural references, and error correction, positioning it as a next‑generation tutor. The reliance on a powerful LLM also means the product inherits the compute‑intensity and carbon footprint concerns associated with AI data centers.

analysis.heading: Regulatory and Ethical Considerations
analysis.content: Because Reeno initiates outbound calls, it falls under telemarketing and consumer‑protection statutes in many jurisdictions, including the U.S. Federal Trade Commission’s rules on unsolicited communications and the EU’s ePrivacy Directive. The app’s data‑handling practices—recording user speech for model improvement—must comply with GDPR, CCPA, and emerging AI‑specific regulations such as the EU AI Act. Open‑source advocates note that Reeno’s core model is not publicly disclosed, limiting external auditability. The company has pledged a “transparent consent flow” that requires users to opt‑in to call‑based practice, but the effectiveness of this mechanism will be scrutinized by regulators and consumer‑rights groups.

analysis.heading: Regional Adoption – Spotlight on Myanmar
analysis.content: Myanmar’s multilingual landscape (Burmese, Shan, Karen, etc.) makes it a fertile market for AI‑driven language tools, especially as internet penetration rises and traditional classroom resources remain scarce. Reeno’s agentic approach could accelerate English proficiency among young professionals, supporting the country’s integration into global supply chains. Yet, the political climate—marked by tight media controls and surveillance—means that any app that records voice data may be subject to government scrutiny. Partnerships with local NGOs or compliance with Myanmar’s nascent data‑protection framework will be critical for sustainable adoption.

key_facts: Reeno initiates random phone calls to practice speaking a chosen language
Powered by a proprietary LLM comparable to OpenAI GPT‑4‑Turbo and Google Gemini
Includes real‑time pronunciation feedback and contextual corrections
Requires explicit opt‑in consent to comply with telemarketing regulations
Targets global learners, with early pilots in Southeast Asia, notably Myanmar
implications: Agentic AI could become a new norm for language acquisition, shifting pedagogical strategies toward spontaneous immersion
Regulators may need to update consent and privacy frameworks to address AI‑initiated voice interactions
Open‑source transparency pressures could push Reeno to disclose model architecture or adopt community‑audited safety layers
items.outlook: If Reeno can balance its innovative agentic design with robust consent mechanisms and transparent data practices, it may set a benchmark for next‑generation educational AI. Success in emerging markets like Myanmar could unlock a sizable user base, while compliance challenges may spur industry‑wide standards for AI‑driven outbound communications. Over the next 12‑18 months, we expect increased scrutiny from regulators, potential collaborations with open‑source communities, and a wave of competitor products that emulate Reeno’s call‑based learning model.
